newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Anti-Japan mood in HK on war anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Japan mood in HK on war anniversary.

text.p: Anti-Japan sentiment whipped up in Hong Kong by Tokyo's claim to a group of disputed islands headed for a new high on Wednesday with rallies and candlelit vigils on the 65th anniversary of Japan's invasion of China.

The date is a painful one in the collective Chinese memory because the invasion of northeast China marked the start of a 14-year military carve-up by Japanese forces, accompanied by a string of war atrocities against Chinese civilians.
The memory is acute in Hong Kong because it was one of the territories occupied by Japan, from 1941 to 1945.

Anti-Japan protests have been steadily growing over the past month, sparked by Japan's renewed claim to the East China Sea island group China calls the Diaoyus and known in Japan as the Senkakus. Both countries claim the islands have been theirs for centuries.
On Wednesday, a group of Hong Kong social workers marched to a Japanese school to demand that Japanese children be taught the truth about Japan's atrocities in World War Two.
They painted a picture of a crumpled Japanese military banner on the ground outside the school and urged pupils to resist a revival of Japanese militarism.

Another protest group marched into a Japanese department store in Hong Kong's prime shopping district of Causeway Bay shouting "don't buy Japanese goods". Management called in the police and evicted the protesters.

Passersby told reporters that they approved of the protests and the boycott call. Ships sounded their horns in Hong Kong harbour at noon as another mark of protest, and protest advertisements appeared in newspapers.
The British colony's biggest political party, the Democratic Party, and other groups planned to stage a rally and candlelit vigil in the evening to mark the invasion anniversary.

Protests in Hong Kong swelled last weekend when more than 10,000 people gathered in the biggest protest action seen in any Chinese-populated territory so far during the campaign. The latest rally on Tuesday night drew 2,000 demonstrators.

Smaller protests have taken place in Taiwan and Macau, but China itself, while chastising Japan, has urged caution and has taken steps to prevent nationalist dissidents from launching a mass movement that might grow out of control.
Campaigners in Hong Kong have gathered more than 760,000 signatures on petitions to protest against Japan's sovereignty claim over the archipelago, the daily Ming Pao reported.
Japan's consulate has been flooded with petitions and protest notes handed over on its doorstep in recent weeks.
Hong Kong activists plan to sail to the islands next week to tear down a lighthouse erected by Japanese rightists.
The wave of patriotic nationalism has united usually opposing political forces, bridging the divide between pro-Beijing groups and anti-communist democrats.

"For the first time since the rift between them started, political activists in Hong Kong and the mainland government are united in a common cause and against a common adversary," one of China's Hong Kong advisers, Tsang Yok-sing, said on Tuesday.
The Beijing-funded, Hong Kong daily Wen Wei Po said in an editorial no country had hurt China more in its recent history than Japan.
The newspaper said Tokyo owed China a lot, while China owed Japan nothing. China was capable, with its 1.2 billion people, of defending itself and peace in the region, it said.
The Japanese government has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and has refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion with China.
Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
